(CNN) -- The investigation of the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestle Toll House cookie dough is nearly over, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The cause of the contamination has not been identified. Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. David Acheson, the FDA's associate commissioner for foods, says the samples of cookie dough his agency has tested do not contain the E. coli strain that sickened 74 people in 32 states. On June 19, Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. Thirty-four people have been hospitalized; no deaths have been reported. The CDC reports that the majority of the patients were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw. Last month, the FDA found E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough, but after testing, investigators found that the strain in the sample did not match the outbreak strain. "We are still in speculation mode," Acheson said, but the E. coli "most likely came from raw ingredients" such as flour. The E.coli strain that caused the outbreak, 0157:H7, is typically found in fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep or goats. Acheson points out that it's not unusual for those animals to be carrying more than one strain of the bacteria. But he believes that the root cause of the contamination may never be known. "We have to conclude we're unlikely to have a definitive determination," he said. Most people with E. coli 0157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection. The FDA notified Nestle USA on Thursday that its investigation at the Danville plant was over. Nestle says FDA inspectors were at the plant for more than a week and found no E. coli on equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the facility after the outbreak. "We've dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli," Nestle USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said. MacDonald announced that Nestle is easing back into production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour and margarine and says it is thoroughly testing the new products and all raw ingredients. Consumers will have to wait to see cookie dough back in grocery stores. "You're not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time," MacDonald said. But when it does appear, the company will mark the cookie dough with a new label that clearly designates it as a new batch. It will also continue to carry a reminder to not eat the dough raw.

In the summer of 2009, a widespread foodborne illness outbreak shocked consumers and turned a beloved household staple into a public health hazard. A total of 74 people across 31 states fell ill after consuming raw, pre-packaged Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough. The outbreak led to dozens of hospitalizations, severe complications such as acute kidney failure, and a massive voluntary recall of millions of cookie dough products. 

Determined to locate the source of the dangerous *Escherichia coli* (E. coli) O157:H7 strain, federal regulators from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) launched an intensive, forensic investigation. Their primary focus was Nestlé’s main production facility in Danville, Virginia, where the implicated cookie dough had been manufactured.

The inquiry at the Danville plant became one of the most exhaustive food safety investigations of its time. Federal inspectors spent weeks meticulously examining the facility, going so far as to dismantle complex industrial production lines piece by piece. Investigators scrubbed machinery, inspected supply channels, and collected samples from every stage of the manufacturing process. In total, regulators conducted over 1,000 tests on factory equipment, environmental surfaces, and raw ingredients—including flour, sugar, pasteurized eggs, butter, and chocolate chips. 

Despite the extraordinary scale of the operation, the investigation yielded perplexing and frustrating results. While laboratory testing did detect *E. coli* in a few isolated samples, none of the bacteria recovered from the plant or its ingredients matched the specific genetic strain responsible for sickening the 74 victims. 

Unable to pinpoint a single smoking gun, the FDA eventually brought its investigation to a close. In its final report, the agency conceded a frustrating truth: the definitive root cause of the contamination will likely never be known.

According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the outbreak was caused by *E. coli* O157:H7, a severe and potentially deadly strain of bacteria. The pathogen produces Shiga toxins, which can trigger severe stomach cramps, bloody diarrhea, and dangerous complications such as Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a form of kidney failure. The outbreak sickened more than 70 people across 35 states, leading to dozens of hospitalizations.

In its report, the FDA confirmed that laboratory testing found the matching strain of *E. coli* in unopened packages of Nestlé Toll House dough produced at the company’s main manufacturing plant in Danville, Virginia. However, inspectors were unable to pinpoint the exact raw ingredient that introduced the bacteria into the facility. 

Because cookie dough is a raw mixture of several agricultural commodities—including flour, butter, eggs, sugar, and chocolate—any one of these unprocessed inputs could have carried the contamination. FDA officials noted that flour was considered a primary suspect, as raw grain is grown outdoors and exposed to animal waste and environmental pathogens before being milled, without undergoing a "kill step" like cooking during initial processing. The investigation highlighted a growing public health concern regarding consumers eating unbaked dough, a common practice despite long-standing warnings.

In light of the FDA's findings, Nestlé announced plans to resume production and restock retail inventory under significantly altered manufacturing processes. To prevent future outbreaks, the company is implementing strict new safety measures, most notably requiring all flour used in its cookie dough to undergo a heat-treatment process designed to eliminate harmful bacteria before it enters the mixing facility.

Additionally, Nestlé has instituted a more rigorous "hold and test" procedure, where raw ingredients and finished batches of dough are screened for pathogens before being cleared for distribution. 

The company is also redesigning its packaging to feature prominent, revised warning labels explicitly advising consumers against eating raw cookie dough and reminding them that the product is formulated strictly to be baked. With these safety overhauls in place, Nestlé confirmed it is reopening the Danville plant, paving the way for Toll House cookie dough to safely return to market shelves.

**SPECIAL REPORT: Inside the Nestlé Toll House Cookie Dough *E. coli* Outbreak**

In the summer of 2009, one of America’s most recognizable household brands became the center of a major public health crisis. Nestlé USA issued a massive voluntary recall of its Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products after federal health agencies linked the popular treat to a nationwide outbreak of *Escherichia coli* (*E. coli*) O157:H7. 

The outbreak marked a turning point in food safety, forcing regulators and manufacturers to recognize raw flour and unbaked dough as significant biological hazards. 

Here is a comprehensive breakdown of the outbreak, the regulatory findings, and the steps Nestlé took to overhaul its operations before returning to store shelves.

---

### 1. The Human Toll: Scope of the Outbreak

The outbreak began coming to light in May and June 2009, when state health departments noticed an unusual spike in *E. coli* O157:H7 infections—a severe strain of the bacteria capable of causing bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal cramps, and kidney failure.

According to final data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):
* **Confirmed Cases:** **80 individuals** were officially confirmed to have been infected with the outbreak strain across **31 states**.
* **Hospitalizations:** At least **35 people** were hospitalized due to the severity of their symptoms.
* **Severe Complications:** **10 patients** developed Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS), a type of kidney failure predominantly affecting young children and the elderly.
* **Demographics:** A overwhelming majority of those sickened were young females—the primary demographic reporting the consumption of raw, unbaked cookie dough prior to falling ill.
* **Fatalities:** Remarkably, no deaths were directly attributed to the outbreak at the time.

While Nestlé had long printed disclaimers on its packaging warning consumers not to eat raw dough, federal health officials noted that the practice was widespread, necessitating a higher standard of safety for products commonly consumed raw.

---

### 2. FDA Findings and the Search for the Contaminant

On June 18, 2009, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the CDC issued a joint warning advising consumers to discard all ready-to-bake Nestlé Toll House refrigerated dough products. Nestlé voluntarily recalled 3.6 million packages of dough that same day.

The FDA launched an extensive investigation into Nestlé’s primary production facility located in **Danville, Virginia**. 

Key findings from the FDA investigation included:
* **Product Testing:** FDA laboratory tests successfully isolated the matching strain of *E. coli* O157:H7 from an unopened package of Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough collected from a consumer's home, definitively linking the product to the outbreak.
* **The Root Cause Mystery:** Identifying the exact source of contamination proved challenging because cookie dough contains multiple raw ingredients (flour, sugar, butter, eggs, chocolate, molasses). 
* **Flour as the Prime Suspect:** While eggs were historically viewed as the primary risk in raw dough (for *Salmonella*), the FDA’s epidemiologic and environmental evidence increasingly pointed toward **raw agricultural flour** as the likely vector for the *E. coli*. Because wheat is grown outdoors, it can be exposed to animal waste containing *E. coli*, which is not eliminated during traditional dry-milling processes.

Inspectors noted that while Nestlé’s Danville facility maintained good manufacturing practices overall, traditional sanitation could not eliminate pathogens introduced by raw, untreated ingredients brought into the plant.

---

### 3. Nestlé’s Remediation: Overhauling Safety Before Relaunch

Before the FDA allowed Nestlé to put its refrigerated cookie dough back on grocery store shelves, the company was required to implement a massive safety overhaul. Nestlé spent millions of dollars restructuring its supply chain and manufacturing protocols to ensure that even if consumers ignored package warnings and ate the raw dough, it would be safe.

Nestlé executed the following major corrective measures:

#### A. Transition to Heat-Treated Flour
The most significant industrial change was Nestlé’s decision to switch entirely to **heat-treated (pasteurized) flour**. By subjecting the raw wheat flour to a specialized thermal process prior to mixing, any potential foodborne pathogens—including *E. coli* and *Salmonella*—are killed before the ingredient ever reaches the manufacturing plant.

#### B. Complete Facility Overhaul and Decontamination
Production at the Danville, Virginia, plant was halted for several weeks. During this time, Nestlé:
* Performed deep-cleaning and sterilization of the entire facility and processing equipment.
* Redesigned equipment to eliminate "dead zones" where moisture or food particles could trap bacteria.
* Restructured plant workflows to strictly segregate raw ingredient handling from finished product mixing areas.

#### C. Rigorous "Hold-and-Test" Protocols
Nestlé established a stringent ingredient-testing regime. Under the new system:
* Raw ingredients were held and tested for pathogens before being accepted into the facility.
* Finished batches of cookie dough were subjected to a "test-and-release" protocol, meaning products were held in warehouses and only shipped to retailers after lab results cleared them of contamination.

#### D. Redesigned Packaging and Warning Labels
While the reformulation rendered the dough significantly safer to eat raw, Nestlé updated its product packaging to feature larger, more prominent warnings explicitly instructing consumers to bake the dough before consuming. (Years later, this paved the way for Nestlé to market explicitly "safe-to-eat-raw" edible cookie dough lines).

---

### 4. The Return to Market and Industry Legacy

In late August 2009—roughly two months after the initial recall—Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough returned to store shelves featuring a prominent **"New Formulation"** label to reassure consumers.

The 2009 Nestlé recall served as a major wake-up call for the broader food industry. It fundamentally shifted how the FDA and food manufacturers viewed raw flour, changing it from a low-risk dry ingredient to a recognized risk factor for foodborne illness. Today, the heat-treatment methods and testing standards pioneered during the 2009 Nestlé remediation remain the standard across the commercial baking industry.

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** Federal health officials announced Thursday that the nationwide *E. coli* outbreak linked to refrigerated pre-packaged cookie dough is officially over, bringing a close to a months-long investigation that sickened dozens of people across the country.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the outbreak of *E. coli* O157:H7 was tied to raw, pre-packaged cookie dough, leading to more than 70 reported illnesses across 35 states. More than half of those infected required hospitalization, though no deaths were reported.

The crisis prompted a massive nationwide recall of Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products and forced the temporary shutdown of the company’s primary manufacturing facility in Danville, Virginia. 

Nestlé collaborated closely with federal inspectors during the probe, completely overhauling its food safety protocols. The company implemented mandatory testing of raw ingredients, upgraded sanitization procedures at its manufacturing plants, and switched to using heat-treated flour designed to kill potential pathogens before products reach store shelves.

Laurie MacDonald, spokeswoman for Nestlé USA, stressed the company’s renewed commitment to consumer safety as products return to retail locations.

"The safety of our consumers is, and always has been, our absolute top priority," MacDonald said. "We have instituted rigorous new testing standards and upgraded our manufacturing processes to ensure that our products meet the highest standards of quality and safety. We are confident in the safety of our products as they return to store shelves."

With the investigation formally closed and new safety measures in place, federal regulators say the immediate public health threat has been resolved. However, health officials urge consumers to remember that raw batter and dough products are intended strictly for baking before consumption.

**FDA Concludes Nestlé Toll House E. Coli Probe Without Pinpointing Source of Contamination**

**WASHINGTON** — Federal health regulators have officially closed their exhaustive, months-long investigation into the nationwide *E. coli* outbreak linked to Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough, concluding the inquiry without identifying the definitive source of the bacterial contamination.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA), working alongside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and state health departments, confirmed that while extensive testing established a clear link between Nestlé’s raw cookie dough and dozens of severe illnesses, exhaustive laboratory testing of raw ingredients at the manufacturing facility failed to yield a positive sample for the pathogen.

### A Widespread Outbreak

The outbreak, which began in early spring, led to a massive nationwide recall in June when Nestlé USA voluntarily pulled more than 3.8 million packages of refrigerated cookie dough products from retail shelves. 

According to final figures released by the CDC, the outbreak sickened at least 72 people across 30 states. More than 30 individuals were hospitalized, and nine developed a severe type of kidney failure known as Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS). No deaths were reported. The vast majority of victims were young women and children, a demographic frequently known to consume unbaked cookie dough.

Epidemiological evidence strongly pointed to the pre-packaged dough. "The statistical association between the illnesses and the consumption of Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough was exceptionally strong," the FDA noted in its final report. Furthermore, public health laboratories isolated the outbreak strain of *E. coli* O157:H7 from open packages of the dough recovered from victims' homes.

### The Search for the Source

Despite tracing the problem to Nestlé's primary processing plant in Danville, Virginia, investigators were unable to pinpoint precisely how the bacteria entered the production line. 

FDA inspectors spent weeks examining the Danville facility, auditing manufacturing procedures, assessing sanitation protocols, and sampling dozens of environmental surfaces. Investigators also aggressively tested the individual raw ingredients used to make the dough, including flour, sugar, pasteurized eggs, margarine, and chocolate chips.

None of the raw ingredients tested positive for the specific *E. coli* O157:H7 strain responsible for the outbreak.

"Food safety investigations of processed, multi-ingredient foods are extraordinarily complex," an FDA spokesperson said during a press briefing. "Because ingredients are sourced from multiple suppliers and processed in large batches, the contaminated lot of raw material may have been entirely used up by the time the outbreak was detected and testing began."

### Flour Emerges as the Primary Suspect

While the FDA's formal conclusion remains unresolved regarding absolute proof, food safety experts and regulators increasingly suspect raw flour was the culprit. 

Historically, public health advice regarding raw dough focused almost exclusively on the risk of *Salmonella* from raw eggs. However, the Nestlé outbreak highlighted raw flour as an underrecognized vector for foodborne illness. Wheat is an agricultural product grown in open fields where it can be exposed to bird, wildlife, or livestock feces. Because milling wheat into flour does not involve a heat treatment—or "kill step"—to destroy pathogens, low levels of bacteria can survive in dry flour for extended periods.

Dr. Robert Tauxe, a senior food safety official at the CDC, noted that the Nestlé investigation marked a turning point in how regulators view low-moisture foods. "This outbreak brought to light the fact that dry ingredients like flour, which we previously considered low-risk for *E. coli*, can indeed harbor dangerous pathogens and cause widespread illness when consumed uncooked," Tauxe said.

### Industry Response and New Safety Standards

In response to the investigation, Nestlé USA implemented significant overhauls to its manufacturing processes and product formulation. 

The company sanitized and temporarily closed the Danville plant during the height of the investigation. Upon reopening, Nestlé permanently transitioned to using heat-treated flour in all of its commercial cookie dough formulations. The heat-treatment process acts as a kill step, neutralizing potential pathogens before the flour is blended into the commercial mix.

Nestlé also redesigned its packaging to feature prominent, mandatory warnings advising consumers not to consume raw dough, emphasizing that the product is intended strictly to be eaten fully baked.

"The safety of our consumers is our highest priority," Nestlé USA said in a statement following the FDA's announcement. "While the definitive source of the contamination could not be established by federal authorities, we have taken proactive, permanent measures—including the implementation of heat-treated flour and enhanced ingredient testing—to ensure that our products meet the highest safety standards moving forward."

### A Persistent Warning to Consumers

With the formal investigation now closed, the FDA reiterates its standing warning to the public: consumer raw dough products should never be eaten unbaked, regardless of the brand.

"This investigation underscores a vital message for home bakers and consumers alike," the FDA stated. "Raw dough, whether purchased at a store or made from scratch at home, is not ready-to-eat. Until it goes through the oven, the risk of foodborne illness remains real."
